To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the asymmetry of vestibular responses in reticulospinals neurons is a factor contributing to the postural disturbances caused by a unilateral lesion of the vestibular labyrinth in the lamprey.
the asymmetry of vestibular responses in reticulospinally projecting neurons is an important factor contributing in the loss of equilibrium of the lamprey after a unilateral labyrinthectomy.
the bilateral asymmetry of vestibular responses in reticulospinale neurons is a cause of the UL-induced rolling of lampreys during swimming.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms of postural control in the lamprey.
the role of the labyrinth in the control of posture of the swimming lamprey.
a comparative analysis of the neural mechanisms of postural control in the lamprey and higher vertebrates.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the asymmetry in the pitch response of the lamprey is caused by an asymmetry of vestibulo-reticulospinal pathways, which in turn is caused by an UL.
UL animals are unable to maintain a stable orientation of the animal body because of a disturbed activity of the posturally important RS neurons.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the lamprey has a bilateral vestibulospinal pathway that controls postural responses to pitch tilts.
the asymmetry of the bilateral activity of RS neurons after UL is a major factor contributing to the postural instability of the lamprey after UL.
the vestibular system is a bilateral system, and it is essential for the postural control of lampreys.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the asymmetry in vestibular responses in lampreys after unilateral labyrinthectomy (U.L.) is caused by a loss of excitatory inputs to RS neurons from the contralaterally damaged labyrinth.
the pitch system of the lampreys is asymmetrical.
the pitch control system in the postural network is asymmetric and that this asymmetry contributes to the UL-induced rolling behavior.
